 Order

Petitioners have filed this petition seeking issuance of writ in the nature of certiorari to quash the notification dated 07.11.2009 produced as per Annexure-E, issued by respondent No.3 and for such other reliefs as the Court deems fit to be granted under the facts and circumstances of case.

2. Heard Sri Vishwanath Hegde, learned counsel for the petitioners and Sri Kirtilata R.Patil, learned High Court Government Pleader for respondent No.3 and Smt.Sharmila M.Patil, learned counsel for respondent Nos.1 and 2.

Perused the materials on record.
3.
Learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the petitioners are the owners in possession of the land measuring 9.36 acres in Sy.No.81/2 of Shinganahalli Village, Dharawad Taluk and District.

Respondents have published the notification dated 07.11.2009, produced as per Annexure-E,
proposing to acquire the land for development of the land for industrial purposes.
Even though, the preliminary notification was issued on 07.11.2009, the final notification was never issued as required under law.

The possession of the property NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 was never taken over and therefore in view of Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 ("L.A.Act" for short) the proposal for acquisition, stands lapsed.
4. Learned counsel submits that Section 11-A of L.A.Act mutatis and mutandis applies to the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966 ("KIAD Act" for short).

He places reliance on the decision of the Co-ordinate Bench of this Court in the case of Rajashekhar Vs. State of Karnataka and others1 in support of his contention, where the decision of the Division Bench of this Court was considered and the preliminary notification issued under KIAD Act was quashed.

entities.text: Rajashekhar Vs. State of Karnataka and others1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Accordingly, he prays for allowing the petition.

5. Learned counsel further submitted that the writ petition was filed in the year 2015 and even if a notification was issued subsequently, that will not cure the defect as the notification issued earlier stood lapsed automatically and prays for allowing the petition in the interest of justice.
6.

Per contra, learned counsel for respondent No.1 and 2 opposing the petition submitted that even though there was W.P.No.201214/2015 disposed of on 24.02.2015 NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 delay in publishing the final notification, the same was issued on 17.02.2024.
The writ petition was filed only to seek quashing the preliminary notification, therefore on publishing the final notification on 17.02.2024, the writ petition becomes infructuous.
Accordingly, it is to be dismissed.

7. Learned counsel further submitted that if the petitioners want to challenge the final notification,
they have to prefer a separate writ petition.
Accordingly, prays for dismissal of the petition.

8. Learned counsel submits that in view of Section 28 (4) of KIAD Act, on publishing the final notification, the land vest with the Government and therefore, the petitioners cannot maintain this petition.

9. Learned High Court Government Pleader for respondent No.3-State submits that the Government Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28303398/
3 proposed to acquire 268 acres of land to be acquired for industrial purposes.
Even though there was delay in publishing the final notification, the fact remains that the final notification is already issued and therefore, the petition is liable to be dismissed.
The undisputed facts of the case are that the preliminary notification was issued by the respondents as per Annexure-E on 07.11.2009.

The writ petition was came to be filed on 06.02.2015, seeking to quash the preliminary notification as there is non-compliance of Section 11-A of L.A.Act. Section 11-A of L.A.Act refers to the period within which an award is to be passed by the Collector and it provides that within two years from the date of publication of the declaration i.e.,
the preliminary notification, if no award is made, the entire proceedings for acquisition of land shall lapse.
11.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Satendra Prasad Jain and others Vs. State of U.P. and others2 categorically held that the prescribed period of two years for making the award shall be treated as substantive/mandatory lest the acquisition itself falls on its breach.

entities.text: Satendra Prasad Jain and others Vs. State of U.P. and others2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 12. Now it is the contention taken by the respondents that since acquisition is under KIADB Act, the provisions of Land Acquisition Act are not applicable and it is only section 28 of KIAD Act, is applicable.

In this regard, learned counsel for AIR 1993 SC 2517 NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 the petitioners places reliance on the decision in Rajashekhar's case (supra), wherein the Co-Ordinate Bench of this Court considered a similar question as to whether the provisions of the L.A.Act applies to the cases where KIADB had issued the notification proposing to acquire the land for its purposes.
It has considered the facts of the said case wherein the preliminary notification was issued, but the final notification was not issued within the statutory period and no award was passed.

The Bench has referred to the Division Bench decision in W.A.No.3189-3201/2010(LA-KIADB) with connected matters, which was referred to in the case of Cheluve Gowda @ Chikkonu Vs. State of Karnataka &
others3 and extracted paragraph Nos.7 and 8, which read as under:
7.

entities.text:
Cheluve Gowda @ Chikkonu Vs. State of Karnataka &
others3
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, the question is no longer res integra.

A division bench of this Court in W.A.Nos.3189-3201 of 2010 (LA-KIADB) connected with W.A.Nos.3202-3206 of 2010 (LA-KIADB) dated 20.11.2012 has addressed the very question and has held thus:
"36.

From the aforesaid discussion, it is clear if a period is prescribed under the Act for issue of a final declaration as well as for passing of the award, if the final declaration is not issued and the award is not passed within the stipulated period, the entire acquisition lapses, unless it is shown by virtue of any order, order of stay or injunction issued by any 2014(2) AKR 41 NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 Court, the authorities were precluded from completing the acquisition proceedings.
It is by operation of law as contained in the statute.
Merely because such a provision is not found in an enactment, it does not mean limitation is not a bar at all.

If such a prescription is not there expressly in any enactment it is not possible to hold that Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28303398/
4

entities.text: Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: such an acquisition has lapsed relying on the provisions contained in the Land Acquisition At.
In other words, the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act cannot be read into the Act or such similar statutes.

But nonetheless in order to decide what is the reasonable time within which authorities have to exercise their power either for issue of a final notification or for passing of the award is concerned, certainly the Parliament intendment as contained in this provision cannot be completely lost sight of.
On the contrary, it acts as a guide.
It expresses the will of the Parliament.
It has to be given due weight.

When this acquisition proceedings were delayed endlessly and land owners were deprived of just compensation under law and consequently the constitutional right was violated, the Parliament amended the Land Acquisition Act prescribing the time limit.
According to the Parliament, one year is the reasonable time for passing of a final declaration and two years is the time for passing of an award.
If within those periods the final declaration is not issued, the award is not passed, the whole acquisition lapses.
The Act is enacted for industrial development which has to be done expeditiously.
Such an industrial development results in generation of employment and economic growth of the State.
If the land is required for such public purpose a special enactment was enacted for speedy acquisition of land.

Merely because the provisions contained in Section 6(1) and 11A is not incorporated in this Act or after the Parliament amended the Land Acquisition Act in 1984, the State NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 legislature did not think it fit to bring in similar provisions under the Act, it does not mean that the State Government can exercise its power for issue of a final declaration or passing of an award without any regard to time limit.
It has to be done within a reasonable time.

As held by the Apex Court in Ram Chand's case (Ram Chand V. Union of India, reported in (1994) 1 SCC 44): (1993 AIR SCW 3479) two years is held to be a reasonable time within which a final declaration has to be issued, if there are no hurdles placed in the acquisition by the land owners or if there are no hurdles in law.

entities.text: Ram Chand V. Union of India, reported in (1994) 1 SCC 44): (1993 AIR SCW 3479)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the final declaration is not issued within two years, certainly the land acquisition has to lapse, notwithstanding the absence of any specific provision in the Act as contained in the Land Acquisition Act.
When we say it is two years or one year it does not mean on expiry of the said two years or one year, as calculated under the L.A.Act, the acquisition has to lapse.
It is roughly two years or one year.
Few days or months this way or that way should not matter.

Except for this absence of mathematical precision in calculating the period,
the substance has to be applied.
The parliamentary intention in prescribing time limit under the L.A.Act cannot be ignored.

However, it all depends on the fact of that particular case, the conduct of the parties, the purpose for which the land is sought to be acquired and the problems faced by the acquiring authorities in concluding the acquisition.

Therefore, it is not possible to accept the contention of the acquiring authority that in the absence of any specific provision under the Act, no such time limit can be imposed and the same is without any substance.

Even in the absence of any such prescriptions expressly under the statute, having regard to the fact that the right to property is a constitutional right and the person whose land is sought to be acquired is entitled to compensation at Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28303398/
5 - 10 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 the market rate, such a compensation has to be paid to him at the earliest and therefore, the power of acquisition should be exercised within a reasonable time so that the person who lost the land is duly compensated at the earliest point of time."

8. In the instant case, the Preliminary Notification under Section 28(1) of the KIAD Act was passed on 15.6.2005 and the Final Notification under Section 28(4) of the Act was passed on 29.1.2007 and it is candidly admitted in the petition that though there was an attempt to arrive at a consensus with the land owners as to the quantum of compensation, there was no finality and the award is yet to be passed.
Therefore, in the light of the law laid down by this Court, the inordinate delay in passing the Award vitiates the acquisition proceedings and accordingly the writ petition is allowed as prayed for.
The impugned proceedings are quashed.
(Emphasis supplied)

13. The Courts have categorically held that when the preliminary notification under Section 28(1) of KIAD Act was issued, and even when the final notification was issued within the statutory period but when the award was not passed within the reasonable time, it is held that in the light of the law laid down by this Court, the inordinate delay in passing the award vitiate the entire acquisition proceedings and the writ petition was came to be allowed.

Thus, position of law is well settled that the provisions of L.A.Act in the matter of applying Sections - 11 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 11-A is equally applicable to the notification issued under KIAD Act.

14. Now it is the contention of the respondents that the final notification under Section 28(4) of KIAD Act is already issued on 17.02.2024 and therefore the present writ petition has rendered infructuous.
But the fact remains that the preliminary notification was issued on 07.11.2009 and the writ petition came to be filed on 06.02.2015.
In-spite of that, a final notification came to be passed only on 17.02.2024.

When it is already held that the prescribed period of two years for making an award shall be treated as substantive/mandatory lest the acquisition itself falls on its breach, the contention taken by the learned counsel for the respondents does not hold good and there cannot be any explanation for the inordinate delay caused in issuance of the final notification that too during pendency of the writ petition.
By publishing the final notification during the pendency of the writ petition, that too after inordinate delay of more than 15 years, the right of the petitioners cannot be undone by the respondents.

This Courts could have appreciated the move of the respondents even if such final notification and - 12 - Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area ... on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28303398/
6 NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 the award was passed at least within a reasonable time after lapse of two years as prescribed.

entities.text: Uppalpati Venkateshwar Rao S/O ... vs The Karnataka Industrial Area
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 15. In view of the above, I am of the opinion that it is a fit case for exercising the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court for issuance of writ in the nature of certiorari to quash not only the preliminary notification dated 07.11.2009 produced as per Annexure-E but also the final notification dated 17.02.2024 produced by the learned counsel for respondent No.1 and 2 insofar as it relates to the land belonging to the petitioners.

The respondents cannot have ride over the citizens who are the owners of small bits of land and make them wait with their fingers crossed, waiting for publication of the final notification and the award at the mercy of the respondents for years together, without any assurance as to when the final notification and the award will be issued.
It is a clear case of violating the constitutional right of the petitioners to own property.

16. The respondents cannot be permitted to play hide and seek by publishing the final notification after the petitioners approaching the Court seeking quashing of the preliminary - 13 - NC: 2024:KHC-D:5342 notification that too, after unexplained delay of more than 15 years.

Hence, I do not find any merits in the defence taken by the respondents, accordingly, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER i) The writ petition is allowed.
ii) The preliminary notification dated 07.11.2009 produced as per Annexure-E and final notification dated 17.02.2024 are hereby quashed, insofar as it relates to the land belonging to the petitioners.
SD/-
